verses.text: Now there was a certain man of Ramathaim Zophim, of the hill country of Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph, an Ephraimite.
He had two wives. The name of one was Hannah, and the name of other Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.
This man went up out of his city from year to year to worship and to sacrifice to Yahweh  of Armies in Shiloh. The two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, priests to Yahweh, were there.
When the day came that Elkanah sacrificed, he gave to Peninnah his wife, and to all her sons and her daughters, portions;
but to Hannah he gave a double portion, for he loved Hannah, but Yahweh had shut up her womb.
Her rival provoked her severely, to irritate her, because Yahweh had shut up her womb.
As he did so year by year, when she went up to Yahweh’s house. Her rival provoked her; therefore she wept, and didn’t eat.
Elkanah her husband said to her, “Hannah, why do you weep? Why don’t you eat? Why is your heart grieved? Am I not better to you than ten sons?”
So Hannah rose up after they had finished eating and drinking in Shiloh. Now Eli the priest was sitting on his seat by the doorpost of Yahweh’s temple.
She was in bitterness of soul, and prayed to Yahweh, weeping bitterly.

She vowed a vow, and said, “Yahweh of Armies, if you will indeed look at the affliction of your servant, and remember me, and not forget your servant, but will give to your servant a boy, then I will give him to Yahweh all the days of his life, and no razor shall come on his head.”
As she continued praying before Yahweh, Eli saw her mouth.
Now Hannah spoke in her heart. Only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard. Therefore Eli thought she was drunk.
Eli said to her, “How long will you be drunk? Get rid of your wine!”
Hannah answered, “No, my lord, I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit. I have not been drinking wine or strong drink, but I poured out my soul before Yahweh.
Don’t consider your servant a wicked woman; for I have been speaking out of the abundance of my complaint and my provocation.”
Then Eli answered, “Go in peace; and may the God  of Israel grant your petition that you have asked of him.”
She said, “Let your servant find favor in your sight.” So the woman went her way, and ate; and her facial expression wasn’t sad any more.
They rose up in the morning early, and worshiped before Yahweh, and returned, and came to their house to Ramah. Then Elkanah knew Hannah his wife; and Yahweh remembered her.
When the time had come, Hannah conceived, and bore a son; and she named him Samuel,  saying, “Because I have asked him of Yahweh.”
The man Elkanah, and all his house, went up to offer to Yahweh the yearly sacrifice, and his vow.
But Hannah didn’t go up; for she said to her husband, “Not until the child is weaned; then I will bring him, that he may appear before Yahweh, and stay there forever.”
Elkanah her husband said to her, “Do what seems good to you. Wait until you have weaned him; only may Yahweh establish his word.” So the woman waited and nursed her son, until she weaned him.
When she had weaned him, she took him up with her, with three bulls, and one ephah  of meal, and a bottle of wine, and brought him to Yahweh’s house in Shiloh. The child was young.
They killed the bull, and brought the child to Eli.
She said, “Oh, my lord, as your soul lives, my lord, I am the woman who stood by you here, praying to Yahweh.
I prayed for this child; and Yahweh has given me my petition which I asked of him.
Therefore I have also given him to Yahweh. As long as he lives he is given to Yahweh.” He worshiped Yahweh there.

footnotes.content: Elkanah's line stretches back through Jeroham, Elihu, Tohu, to Zuph—names that root him in Ephraim's history. Notice how the text takes time to anchor him: he is not rootless, even though the years ahead will test his faith. A man known by his fathers is a man who can stand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two wives, one house—and one of them carries the ache of empty arms. The text says simply: Peninnah had children, Hannah had none. No softening of it. The Lord sets us in real sorrows, not imaginary ones.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Year by year they journeyed to Shiloh, to the house of Yahweh of Armies—Shiloh, where the ark rested before Jerusalem, where the prayers of Israel rose like smoke. Even in the darkest part of Hannah's story, she kept climbing that road to worship. The house of the Lord was still her father's house.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Watch what Elkanah does: he portions out the sacrifice feast with arithmetic precision. To Peninnah and her children, portions. The custom of the day allowed it. But the law of the heart is older than custom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He loved Hannah, so he gave her double. And yet—Yahweh had shut her womb. His love is large enough to offer what he cannot grant. There is a kind of faithfulness in a man who loves what he cannot fix, and stays.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peninnah provoked her severely, year after year. Some sorrows are sharpened by another's hand. Hannah carried not just barrenness but the sting of rivalry every time she climbed to worship. Yet she climbed anyway.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As he did so year by year—Peninnah's mockery was not a one-time wound but a yearly returning of the knife. The repetition wore her down. She wept, didn't eat. Yet in verse 9, we see her rise again from that very grief.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Am I not better to you than ten sons?" Elkanah speaks from a good heart, but he cannot give what he does not hold. A husband's love is worth more than a household of children—and yet it is not the same thing. Some longings cannot be fixed by another's devotion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After the feasting, Hannah rose. Not before, not in the middle—after. She had swallowed down her grief enough to wait. Eli sat by the doorpost of the temple—the keeper at the threshold, though he did not know what was about to pass through it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In bitterness of soul, she prayed. Not in happiness. Not in victory. In the very place of her breaking, she brought her whole weight to the Lord. There is something about the bottom of a well that makes prayer true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She vowed: if He grants me a son, I will give him back to You. A Nazirite from birth—no razor on his head, set apart from his first breath. She did not ask to keep what she would receive. She asked for it only to surrender it. That is the posture of the deepest prayer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eli saw her mouth moving. He watched a woman at prayer and did not know what he was seeing. Many of us have stood near another's deepest moment without recognizing it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hannah spoke in her heart. Only her lips moved; her voice was not heard. The temple was loud with feasting, and she was silent—a woman crying without a sound. Yet the Lord heard every word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eli thought she was drunk. The old priest mistook desperation for drunkenness. How often we misname what we see in another's face—calling surrender weakness, calling hunger excess.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit," Hannah says plainly. Not proud, not excusing herself. She names it—sorrow. And she tells him the truth: I have poured out my soul. Sometimes being misunderstood gives us the chance to speak plainly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She asks not to be thought wicked, to not be condemned for her complaint. Even in her anguish, she seeks the blessing of being believed. The Lord knew the truth. Eli came to know it too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eli answered: Go in peace. The words of a priest speaking blessing over a broken heart—the old formula of dismissal became, in that moment, a promise. The God of Israel will grant your petition. He did not know what he was speaking into being.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She went away, and ate; her face was no longer sad. Not because her prayer was answered yet—the child had not been conceived. But because she had believed. Something shifted in her when she believed it was given.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They worshiped before Yahweh and returned home to Ramah. Then Elkanah knew Hannah. Then Yahweh remembered her. See the order: worship, intimacy, and remembrance. The promise kept its time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She bore a son and named him Samuel—He has asked of the Lord. The name carries her prayer in it. Her vow spoken in bitterness had become a son's name, calling him back to the God who had heard her. What we give to the Lord returns in a name.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elkanah went up with all his household to pay his yearly vow and sacrifice. The custom of the pilgrimage continued. But this year, something was different.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hannah did not go. She said to her husband: I will bring him when he is weaned. There is a mother's knowledge in this—the season of my keeping before the season of my gift. She would hold him only as long as she must, then give him over.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elkanah said: Do what seems good. Wait. May Yahweh establish His word. And she waited, nursing her son. There is a kind of love that knows how to delay itself, how to hold what it will release. She kept him close for these months, knowing they were all the holding she would have.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When she had weaned him, she took him to Shiloh with three bulls, an ephah of meal, and a bottle of wine—a generous offering. She brought the substance of her household to the Lord's house, not empty-handed but laden with gratitude.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They killed the bull and brought the child to Eli. The sacrifice was made. The threshold was crossed. She could not take him back now.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "As your soul lives, my lord, I am the woman who stood by you here, praying." Hannah spoke her name back into Eli's memory. The woman he had misunderstood was also the woman whose prayer had been answered. She needed him to know.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I prayed for this child, and Yahweh has given me my petition. She says it plainly—no apology, no hiding. This is what the Lord does. This is what He did for me.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As long as he lives he is given to Yahweh. Readers today hear an echo in these words—a mother letting go of what she loved most, knowing He loves him more. We see in Hannah's surrender a shadow of the Father's own gift of His Son to the world. As of 2026-10, that echo still moves the heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
